title: Someone worth following

sections.title: A want that leads into play
sections.text: Begin with a person who wants something they cannot secure alone. In this example, Arda repairs canal gates and wants to find the teacher who left a warning inside a broken mechanism. She has a reason to travel, a useful trade, and a question she can bring to companions. Those details offer more than a title such as warrior or mage. They tell the table why she will examine a gate, protect a worker, or keep following a difficult lead after the first reward has been spent.

sections.title: Three promises, not twenty powers
sections.text: Write one ordinary competence, one extraordinary ambition, and one connection. Arda knows gate machinery, wants to direct existing water, and trusts a courier who carries news between the settlements. Ordinary competence gives the DM material for the world; applicable practices resolve meaningful uncertainty. The extraordinary ambition needs actual acquired permissions. The connection gives another player a place to contribute. A starting concept need not mechanically realize every future possibility. Keep later ambitions in a separate note, so a sentence about someday commanding a river does not become an unstated current power.

sections.title: Choose what matters first
sections.text: Ask what the opening adventure is likely to involve. A flooded workshop favors understanding currents, noticing failing supports, and helping people move. A political journey can make negotiation and evidence more urgent. These are priorities, not locked careers. Choose a foundation and purchases that let you participate in those scenes, then explain each actual rule. The character can remain recognizable when their methods grow. A new training grant need not replace the gatekeeper story; it may show what the gatekeeper learned from being listened to at a difficult meeting.

sections.title: Give the party an invitation
sections.text: Offer a connection other players can accept or alter: you need their map, you repaired their home, or you both want the same missing person found. Do not write another character’s feelings without asking. At the first table conversation, explain one thing Arda can contribute and one thing she cannot yet do. Someone may supply the missing sense, tools, or social approach. Cooperation begins as a shared opportunity, rather than a compulsory distribution of combat roles. A character becomes easier to play when their next useful choice is visible.

sections.title: A conversation before choosing ingredients
sections.text: Player: “I want Arda to understand the gate and help people cross when it fails.” DM: “Does she command water already, or is that what she wants to learn?” Player: “She can redirect existing water under her acquired rules. Creating it is outside the starting idea.” Companion: “Then my rope and route knowledge can help where there is no water.” This example identifies a current contribution, a limit, and a connection. It does not demand a perfect catalogue choice before play. The table can now inspect the actual permissions and propose a manageable starting build, rather than trying to price every future scene the concept suggests.

sections.title: The same person in a dry settlement
sections.text: Change the opening adventure to a dry settlement with a damaged hoist. Arda’s water working may be less immediately useful, but her trade, practical questions, connections, and other actual acquisitions remain relevant. She can examine the mechanism, ask workers about the failure, or help someone reach an ordinary tool. Do not invent water because the character’s theme needs a starring moment. Equally, do not make her irrelevant merely because the most visible extraordinary method is unavailable. Ask what the person wants here and which ordinary or acquired contribution fits. A robust concept supplies reasons to participate beyond one favorable environment.

sections.title: The exercise: a scene without your favorite power
sections.text: Write a place where your favorite working cannot provide its usual result. Then describe one question your character would ask, one ordinary contribution, and one invitation to another party member. For Arda, a dry workshop could prompt “Who used this gate last?”, inspection of a visible damaged hinge, and an offer to support someone while they examine the upper mechanism. Explain why each belongs to her rather than merely naming a generic action. The answer shows whether the concept gives a human something to play. If it does not, add a useful interest or connection before buying several more extraordinary permissions.

imagePurpose: Show companions making different useful contributions at the same table. The illustration supports the choices in the prose; it is not a set of prescribed classes.

quickFacts.label: Starting point
quickFacts.value: A purpose, a contribution, and a connection.

quickFacts.label: Mechanical promise
quickFacts.value: Only the actual acquired rules establish extraordinary behavior.

title: The rope already in your hands

sections.title: Look before inventing
sections.text: A balcony support has cracked. A coil of rope lies beside a canal hook, and an intact post stands on the lower landing. Before proposing an extraordinary solution, ask what those objects can do. Can the rope reach? Can the post take a load? Can someone hear the stranded worker? These questions are ordinary interaction with a described place. The DM can give evident facts directly. A new capability purchase is not required before you may tie a rope or ask someone to take its free end.

sections.title: Make the tool change the stakes
sections.text: In this worked example, a player secures the rope before crossing the damaged stair. The group agrees that a slip could now leave the rescuer suspended rather than immediately falling into the canal. The rope has changed the practical situation. It has not automatically supplied advantage, a fixed bonus, or invulnerability. A suitable check can still resolve meaningful uncertainty, with the new stakes established before commitment. Another scene may have a rotten anchor or a rope that cannot support the load. Describe the actual preparation instead of treating rope as a universal exception.

sections.title: Use extraordinary access where it helps
sections.text: A water shaper supports the stair while the rescuer handles the rope. The support needs its real subject, behavior, reach, and continuing terms. The rope needs its actual length, anchor, and use. Neither contribution erases the other. If the water working ends, the rope can still matter. If the post breaks, owning Water does not silently replace it with an indestructible anchor. Combining ordinary tools and acquired access often produces a more understandable plan than a single broad claim to solve everything magically.

sections.title: Bring the useful record
sections.text: On the equipment line, note what the object is, whether it is carried or equipped, its quantity, Load, final slot requirement, and any actual item rule. Keep Item BU separate from character purchases and ordinary market value. A tool without extraordinary ingredients can remain extremely useful. After the rescue, inspect the rope and recover the hook if possible. These are objects in the shared scene, not disappearing props. The party’s next choice may depend on having a sound rope rather than a longer list of named powers.

sections.title: A conversation about the anchor
sections.text: Player: “I loop the rope around that post before crossing.” DM: “The post is loose in its socket. You can see it move when you pull.” Companion: “There is a sound iron ring on the lower wall. Can we route the line through it instead?” Player: “Yes, if it reaches.” The table is now checking a practical method, not assigning a secret universal bonus to equipment. A visible weakness gives the players a chance to revise before committing. The new route still needs its actual geometry and use established. Preparation becomes rewarding because objects retain understandable properties instead of changing only after a failed roll.

sections.title: The tool is missing next time
sections.text: At a later crossing, the party has left its rope with workers at the first site. That earlier choice matters. It does not forbid the group from acting; they can borrow equipment, search for another route, improvise an available line if suitable, or use an eligible extraordinary method. The DM can explain the practical uncertainty of the alternative. Avoid treating the inventory as both unlimited when a tool would help and irrelevant when it was deliberately lent away. Record the promise to recover it. A missing tool can create a useful social or logistical scene without imposing a mandatory penalty that the rules never established.

sections.title: The exercise: describe what the object changes
sections.text: Choose a lantern, map, hook, or flask from the illustration. Give it an actual use in the rescue and say what changes as a result. A lantern can reveal the broken support, but does not provide unrestricted sight through walls. A map can identify a second approach, but does not prove that the route is still intact. A hook can give a line an anchor if the material and position permit it. The explanation should name a practical relationship. If your answer says only “gain a bonus,” return to the scene and ask what the character is actually doing with the object.

imagePurpose: Place the transparent rope, hook, flask, map, and lantern beside the task sequence. Each object is explicitly used by the example, so the spot art functions as an equipment inventory.

quickFacts.label: Preparation
quickFacts.value: State what the tool changes before the roll.

quickFacts.label: Accounting
quickFacts.value: Item BU, ordinary value, Load, and equipped slots are different figures.

title: A heritage is a history you can use

sections.title: Choose whose story it is
sections.text: Consider a family of bridge couriers who remember each delivery through carved tokens. A player wants that upbringing for a living character; another imagines a tireless ancestral porter still protecting one unfinished parcel. Both images can be compelling. Neither image is a complete mechanical record. Ask which parts belong to ancestry, which come from learned work, and which represent the character’s present role. Lineage, Upbringing, and Manifest give those meanings a place without requiring exactly one prescribed package of each.

sections.title: Name the actual inheritance
sections.text: In this example, the courier’s upbringing organizes a bought practice proficiency, a narrow subject permission, and an eligible verb permission. Their readable definitions and prices remain in the purchase ledger. The upbringing also describes tokens, manners, and remembered roads. Those descriptive details enrich play without automatically granting every language, permanent endurance, or knowledge of all routes. If the player wants an actual exceptional memory or a special movement mode, author its subject, scope, limits, and proposed price openly. A tradition’s name cannot supply a hidden mechanical package.

sections.title: Let two people interpret it differently
sections.text: One courier considers every delivery a sacred obligation. Another wants to expose the patron who misuses that tradition. The same acquired training can support both characters. A heritage need not dictate morality, profession, appearance, or a permanent destiny. Talk about how a player will inhabit it, and leave other members room to differ. When adapting a shared heritage, identify the changed ingredients and adopted version. Changing a paragraph about customs is different from replacing a bought permission with an unrelated new ability.

sections.title: Test it in a living scene
sections.text: A porter blocks a damaged passage because a parcel must not be lost. The party can help fulfill the duty, offer a safer route, or examine who is supposed to receive it. This makes the heritage meaningful through choices. Do not assume the figure must fight because of its appearance, or that its pictured body provides unlisted defenses. For your own character, write one obligation they welcome and one they question. Review any actual drawback separately before claiming mirror credit. A story creates opportunities; accounting records eligible acquisitions.

sections.title: A conversation about the family promise
sections.text: Player: “The couriers say no delivery is abandoned. I want that to matter.” DM: “Is it a value your character tries to honor, or an actual restriction you want to acquire?” Player: “For now it is a value. I may choose differently when a delivery hurts someone.” Companion: “Then I can challenge the tradition without telling your character what they must feel.” The table has separated history from a mechanical drawback. If the player later proposes an actual restriction, its terms and any eligible credit need review. The descriptive promise remains meaningful even when it does not change a number or remove access.

sections.title: One tradition, a different mechanical expression
sections.text: Another character from the same couriers is a maker of protective containers, not a water shaper. They can share customs, relatives, and remembered roads while purchasing different ingredients. A shared heritage may be adapted openly to reflect that difference. State which version or composition was adopted, what rules changed, and what price was agreed. Do not claim that the common name grants both characters every possible courier ability. A specific history can inspire many mechanically distinct people. This is useful when a group wants a coherent background without reducing everyone to copies of one mandatory ancestry package.

sections.title: The exercise: history and current rule
sections.text: Write three sentences about your heritage: a remembered custom, an actual acquired contribution, and a personal response to that custom. For a bridge courier, the custom might be carving a token for each delivery; the contribution might be a reviewed practice grant; the response might be refusing deliveries that endanger children. Explain which sentence changes the mechanical record. Only the actual acquired rule does so unless another explicit consequence has been agreed. The other sentences still create choices and relationships. This distinction lets heritage matter in the story without turning every attractive descriptive detail into an unpriced hidden benefit.

imagePurpose: The porter’s preserved delivery evokes duty carried across generations. Use it beside the example of inherited work and chosen obligation, without implying that undead appearance grants mechanics.

quickFacts.label: Narrative container
quickFacts.value: Lineage, Upbringing, and Manifest organize actual content.

quickFacts.label: A useful test
quickFacts.value: Explain a normal contribution without relying on the heritage’s title.

title: Ask the question that opens the scene

sections.title: Start from what everyone can perceive
sections.text: The DM describes a worker stranded above a canal, a leaning stair, water in a trough, and a rope on the bank. You do not need to memorize the whole handbook to begin. Ask about the nearest sound support, the worker’s condition, and the route between you. Evident information helps the table make choices. A roll is useful when its result answers meaningful uncertainty, not as a compulsory fee before every described object can enter your plan.

sections.title: Say the result before the method
sections.text: “I want the worker safely on the bank” gives the conversation a clear goal. “I roll Mysticism” does not yet tell anyone what is attempted. Now choose a method: support the stair with existing water, send a rope, bring a ladder, or persuade the worker to use another exit. These methods raise different access and risk questions. The DM and players can select a resolution only after the attempt is understandable. Your actual combined bonus is applied once if a check is needed.

sections.title: Make room to revise
sections.text: The player proposes holding a water path while leaving the bank to fetch the worker. The table points out that this particular maintained path requires continued direction. The player can stay and ask a companion to cross, propose a different lasting construction, or choose the rope route instead. Clarification is useful before commitment. It should not become a trap revealed only after the player has accepted a roll. The Rule of Cool gives an exciting idea a fair hearing while keeping its scope and consequences understandable.

sections.title: Follow the changed situation
sections.text: Suppose the stair breaks, but the secured rope keeps the rescuer from falling away. The next choice begins from that new position. Someone can steady the line, negotiate a greater effort, or guide the worker through a window. Do not keep rolling an unchanged sentence until the die finally cooperates. Apply the agreed result, record actual resources and consequences, then ask what is possible now. A scene becomes a shared story when each result changes the next decision, including results that do not deal damage.

sections.title: A conversation with a first-time player
sections.text: Player: “I do not know which rule to use. I want to help the worker.” Companion: “What can you reach from the bank?” DM: “The line and the sound post are beside you.” Player: “I secure the line and call for the worker to take it.” The table can now discuss the actual attempt. The player has contributed without first reciting a family or tier. If the method needs extraordinary access, someone can help locate the relevant acquired rule. New players should be able to begin with a human description and learn the formal language through a situation that makes its purpose clear.

sections.title: The same intent, a different relationship
sections.text: Change the scene: the stranded worker refuses the party’s help because the last rescue left them owing an impossible debt. The physical route can remain available while the social problem changes. The group might explain its offer, bring a trusted witness, or ask what would make assistance acceptable. Influence can support a meaningful attempt, but it does not automatically control the worker’s choices. The rescue is still the objective. A useful plan may now require understanding why someone refuses rather than increasing output. This comparison shows how a single intent can invite different methods without becoming a compulsory sequence of combat actions.

sections.title: The exercise: ask before selecting a roll
sections.text: Choose an uncertain scene and write your intended result in one sentence. Then ask two questions about facts that would influence the method. For the rescue, “Is the post sound?” and “Can the worker take the rope?” are useful because their answers alter the plan. “What do I roll?” is useful only once the actual attempt is clear. Explain which uncertainty the eventual resolution will answer. If you cannot say, revise the question. The aim is not to avoid dice; it is to give the dice a meaningful job and help every participant understand what the result changes.

imagePurpose: Use the rescue scene to annotate visible resources, intended outcome, and two alternative routes. The image makes the players’ questions concrete rather than decorating a generic introduction.

quickFacts.label: The opening sentence
quickFacts.value: Describe what you want to change.

quickFacts.label: Before commitment
quickFacts.value: Access, scope, uncertainty, stakes, and resolution must be intelligible.

title: Enough permission for the next idea

sections.title: Do not shop for an entire universe
sections.text: A player wants to get a companion through a blocked doorway. Start with that intended result rather than purchasing every family whose name seems relevant. Can the obstruction be moved with tools? Can the occupant be persuaded? Is there another route? Ordinary circumstances may support the task. If the plan needs an extraordinary change, identify its actual subject and behavior. A character’s required owned positive verb and domain access establishes a foundation, not a promise that every imagined solution is already available.

sections.title: Read the bound subject
sections.text: Grounded Water concerns that subject. It does not give the meanings of every Tier I domain because its reference price matches theirs. A permission involving a threshold might describe an ordinary door, a spatial boundary, or a symbolic entry condition; those are different authored rules. Inspect the actual definition. The seedling in this example protects a particular entry. Its illustration tells you what you can see, while its actual record determines any exceptional behavior. A dramatic silhouette cannot fill a missing permission.

sections.title: Distinguish a stretch from a different action
sections.text: Redirecting more of an existing stream can increase scale and pressure within a suitable permission. Restoring a dead person introduces a different behavior; adding water or output dice alone does not establish it. Likewise, forcing a hinge, reshaping it, and rewriting who is allowed through are different changes. Higher payment does not automatically purchase that difference during execution. You may acquire a reviewed new rule or ask for an explicit contextual exception, but make the new agreement clear before relying on it.

sections.title: Keep a useful boundary note
sections.text: For a frequent working, write one normal use, one ambitious use, and one outside-scope use. A doorway guide might find a visible safe route, attempt a difficult crossing with consequences, and fail to explain passage through an unknown sealed wall. These tests help the table recognize what has actually been acquired. The purpose is to support future improvisation, not freeze the character into three buttons. A readable boundary tells you which new question to ask when a surprising scene arrives.

sections.title: A conversation at the protected entry
sections.text: Player: “Can my permission move the threshold aside?” DM: “Which subject does your actual domain cover?” Player: “Grounded Water. I imagined the guardian’s doorway as a kind of flow.” DM: “That image is evocative, but it does not make this stone doorway water. You could work with the channel beside it.” The player may propose a route through the channel, speak with the guardian, or review a different acquired rule. This example separates metaphor from permission without dismissing the idea’s spirit. A vivid description can introduce a plan; the actual subject and behavior establish what that plan can change.

sections.title: When the object belongs to the domain
sections.text: Compare a doorway blocked by a sheet of existing water. Now Water is genuinely relevant, but the verb, arrangement, reach, and opposition still matter. The player should describe whether they want to redirect, hold apart, remove, or transform it. Those are not interchangeable because the subject matches. If an acquired permission covers the proposed change, appraise this particular expression. If it does not, discuss an ordinary route or a reviewed extension honestly. The distinction protects a useful narrow foundation while allowing surprising applications wherever its real rule fits, rather than treating every boundary as a refusal to improvise.

sections.title: The exercise: change one ingredient
sections.text: Take your frequent working and replace only its subject: water becomes stone, a visible object becomes a person’s belief, or a known path becomes an unknown destination. Which replacement fits the acquired definition, and which introduces a different permission? Explain the result from the actual text. A shared tier or suggested price is not proof of equivalence. Next restore the original subject and increase only its eligible scale. That change may need a different appraisal and consequence, but it does not necessarily ask for a new kind of behavior. The comparison teaches you to name what truly changed in an ambitious proposal.

imagePurpose: The guardian at a narrow entrance provides a concrete distinction between ordinary passage, a granted exceptional method, and a permission that still has boundaries.

quickFacts.label: Permission
quickFacts.value: Read the actual subject and behavior.

quickFacts.label: Scale
quickFacts.value: More of an eligible result does not supply an unrelated result.

title: Build a working you can read aloud

sections.title: Begin with the ordinary sentence
sections.text: A courier wants to guide existing water around a damaged support. Write that sentence first. Then identify the acquired ingredients that support it: the bound Water subject, a suitable verb, and any acquired reach or arrangement actually needed. The player may already own them. The useful question is what each contributes, not how many layers of containers a record can display. A simple readable primitive remains valid without first being wrapped in an effect and capability.

sections.title: Use a layer for a reason
sections.text: An effect can gather related ingredients that recur together. A capability can explain a complete working or ready intent. A heritage can connect these acquisitions to the courier’s history. These layers should make a reader’s job easier. For example, Guided Water identifies the recurring ingredients, and River Hand explains how they support directing a stream. A second capability can reuse those ingredients while describing another eligible expression. Its name does not automatically buy another occurrence, add a new behavior, or create another simultaneous action.

sections.title: Separate permission from this use
sections.text: The reusable record says what is available. The actual attempt says which water, which path, which recipient, and what pressure applies now. In a quiet room, transferring water between bowls may be secure. Around a failing bridge, the same access meets urgency, obstacles, and people who need to cross. Record a helpful normal example, but leave the table room to appraise a changed expression. An output die does not turn every rearrangement into an attack or healing effect.

sections.title: Read the whole chain once
sections.text: Before play, ask someone else to read the capability and its ingredient definitions. Can they say what happens, how a target is located, what ends the result, and what remains outside its scope? If the answer requires chasing several titles that repeat the same vague sentence, simplify. Keep version references where they matter, while reproducing enough actual rules for paper play. The goal is a working a human can explain, not a decorative hierarchy whose most important clause is missing from every layer.

sections.title: A conversation over the working card
sections.text: Player: “River Hand contains Guided Water, and Guided Water points to these acquired ingredients.” Companion: “What does it actually do now?” Player: “I direct this existing flow around the damaged support, within the stated reach.” Companion: “Does it hold when you leave?” Player: “Not under this version’s continuing terms.” The companion has tested an important practical boundary. The nested record should make that answer easy to find. It need not reproduce every heading in a catalogue, but it should preserve the actual definitions and recipient conditions on which this attempt depends. A clear capability is something another human can interrogate.

sections.title: A second capability from the same ingredients
sections.text: The player also writes a working for guiding water between vessels. It can refer to the same acquired subject and verb permissions while describing a different eligible use. Those references do not grant a second simultaneous Main Intent or another purchase credit. Read whether the arrangement needs anything additional and what one declared execution would involve. The new capability is useful because it makes a recurring task easier to explain. It should not claim that every familiar ingredient applies to every circumstance simply because the composition looks tidy. A reusable pattern remains anchored in the ingredients’ real scope.

sections.title: The exercise: remove a decorative layer
sections.text: Choose a composition with several nested titles. Remove one layer temporarily and read the actual rules beneath it. Did you lose a genuine instruction, or only a repeated heading? If the instruction was genuine, give it an identifiable place in the record. If it was repeated decoration, simplify the path a reader follows. Then ask someone to explain one normal use and one changed use from the revised card. The answer should not rely on already knowing your character. This exercise improves paper play and conversation because the construction’s essential behavior survives even when the surrounding interface is absent.

imagePurpose: Use the makers’ table as a construction metaphor, then pair it with ingredient labels supplied by the layout. The picture supports assembly; the text explains reference identity.

quickFacts.label: Useful layers
quickFacts.value: Effect: reusable grouping. Capability: understandable working.

quickFacts.label: Paper check
quickFacts.value: Keep actual ingredient definitions available, not only their names.

title: One purchase, several arrangements

sections.title: Count what was acquired
sections.text: Suppose you acquire one domain permission and refer to it inside an effect, a capability, and an upbringing. There is still one owned acquisition in the purchase ledger. The containers organize it. They do not multiply its price or produce several additional automatic contributions. When you deliberately acquire another eligible occurrence, give that occurrence its own identity and review the actual stacking rules. Card count, paragraph count, and ownership count are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Name the figures clearly
sections.text: Keep progression allowance, positive acquired BU, ordinary unspent BU, available mirror credit, and actual debt used distinct. The debt ceiling is a limit, not free credit. A descriptive inconvenience is not automatically an eligible mirror. Item BU has its own ledger. Execution Cost is an agreed consequence of using a working, not a second purchase of all its ingredients. These distinctions let a player reorganize a character’s story without accidentally doubling purchases or treating unused credit as ordinary spare budget.

sections.title: Watch the repeated tool analogy
sections.text: A rope can appear in your crossing plan, rescue plan, and campsite notes while remaining the same rope. If it breaks in one scene, the others do not each retain a free intact copy. Reused acquired permissions are not consumable rope, but the analogy helps you identify one underlying occurrence rather than three separate titles. Its active contribution follows the rule’s scope and conditions. Two references to the same +2 clause do not automatically become +4.

sections.title: Audit a revised build
sections.text: After changing a capability or moving content into a heritage, read the acquisition ledger again. Which actual ingredients were added, removed, or replaced? Which are references to what you already own? Have item mechanics slipped into the character ledger? Does an accepted personal drawback still apply to its actual recipient? Record the change openly with the table. A clearer composition can be valuable without changing the spent total at all, while a genuinely new ingredient needs an acquisition and its agreed accounting.

sections.title: A conversation at the purchase ledger
sections.text: Player: “I have the same Water occurrence inside two capabilities. Do I count it twice?” DM: “Not merely because it is referenced twice. Which actual occurrence did you acquire?” Player: “This one, with the same definition and identity.” Companion: “Then each capability should point to that occurrence. A separate acquired modifier would need its own entry.” The conversation is about ownership, not typography. Two attractive cards do not prove two purchases, just as one compressed card can contain several genuine acquisitions. The ledger makes the difference visible, letting the group reorganize the record without using container count as a budget calculation.

sections.title: When there really are two sources
sections.text: Compare two distinct acquired rules that both contribute to a practice under their actual conditions. They are not duplicates merely because their effects resemble each other; applicable sources stack by default unless their authored restrictions say otherwise. Check whether either is unique, conditional, or otherwise limited. A repeated reference to one occurrence remains different from two genuine eligible sources. Explain the contributing entries to the table before adding their results. The purpose is to count honestly, not assume that everything with a similar name is prohibited or that every repeated paragraph must produce another bonus.

sections.title: The exercise: trace a reference
sections.text: Choose one primitive in a capability and follow it to the purchase ledger. Write its identity, actual rule, agreed price, and every composition that refers to it. Now add a second capability that uses the same occurrence. The acquisition total should not change solely because of that new reference. Next imagine adding a genuinely new ingredient with a different rule. That addition needs its own acquisition and accounting. Explain both changes aloud. The exercise gives you a practical way to spot accidental double counting while preserving real stacking where the acquired definitions support it. Review any item source separately in its own ledger.

imagePurpose: Arrange the pictured tools beside a ledger-and-reference diagram. Each object is counted once while appearing in several uses, making the ownership distinction tangible.

quickFacts.label: Count once
quickFacts.value: References do not repurchase an owned acquisition.

quickFacts.label: Keep separate
quickFacts.value: Character BU, Item BU, and execution consequences.

title: Choose the question, then the practice

sections.title: Four approaches to one machine
sections.text: A maintenance unit keeps trying to dismantle a cart because its old work order calls the load salvage. In this example, a character can notice which parts it reaches for, analyze its route, remember an obsolete marking, or persuade the depot keeper to suspend the order. These are different intended contributions. Awareness, Reason, Knowledge, and Influence describe useful approaches, but naming a practice does not itself create a result. Tell the table which uncertainty you want to resolve.

sections.title: Ordinary competence remains available
sections.text: You may examine a marking without being trained in every relevant practice. Proficiency adds the applicable PB; it is not permission to attempt ordinary thinking. Extraordinary results still need their actual access. A person with excellent Reason does not automatically read the machine’s hidden memories. Someone trained in Influence does not gain mind control. A practical character can help by holding a cover open, finding a witness, or protecting the cart while another person pursues a different question.

sections.title: Use the displayed total once
sections.text: The default check uses the current relevant attribute, applicable training, and modifiers. If your record already shows their combined practice bonus, add that total once to the selected resolution die. A conditional numerical bonus needs its actual condition; advantage changes which die is selected under the stacking rule. Expertise uses twice PB where granted. Repeated proficiency grants do not repeatedly add training. These contributions can all have places in a scene, but they must not be folded into one unexplained number twice.

sections.title: Let an answer change the task
sections.text: The characters discover that the work order names a different cart. Their next choice is whether to show the correct marking, fetch the keeper, or move the threatened load. They do not need to win every practice in succession before the discovery becomes real. If a result leaves uncertainty, say what is still unknown. If the evidence makes a conclusion secure, the DM can resolve it directly. Practices help you engage with a changing situation; they are not a compulsory sequence of checks before interaction is allowed.

sections.title: A conversation that changes the practice
sections.text: Player: “I use Reason to make the unit accept my order.” DM: “What are you showing it?” Player: “I compare the cart number with its work order.” DM: “Then you are analyzing a mismatch. If you want to persuade the keeper afterward, describe that as a separate contribution.” The distinction does not force a prescribed chain of rolls. It clarifies the question being answered now. The discovered mismatch might make the keeper’s choice secure, or leave a real disagreement. Practices follow the attempt’s meaning, so the player can choose a method before the table selects applicable training and resolution.

sections.title: Bias changes selection, not the combined total
sections.text: In a separate worked example, three applicable advantage sources and one disadvantage source cancel to two remaining advantage stacks. Roll three resolution dice and keep the highest, then apply the relevant combined bonus once. Do not add that bonus to a selected die and again as a separate practice contribution. With opposing net disadvantage, keep the lowest instead; with no net stack, use one die. Each source still needs its actual condition and stacking eligibility. A decorative label saying “careful” does not automatically become another advantage source. Read the record that genuinely grants the contribution.

sections.title: The exercise: the method after the clue
sections.text: The unit recognizes the mismatch but still needs authorization to stop. Write two possible next methods. One might fetch the keeper who can change its instructions; another might physically protect the cart while a companion examines the control. Explain what each method seeks to establish and what it does not. The first does not automatically control the keeper’s decision; the second does not silently confer command of the unit’s internal workings. A useful answer names an actual contribution and the remaining uncertainty. The exercise keeps practice choices grounded in a changing situation rather than treating a favorable total as permission to demand any result.

imagePurpose: The maintenance unit and its work-order dispute anchor the distinction between noticing, reasoning, recalling, and persuading. Its appearance is evidence in the scene, not an automatic combat challenge.

quickFacts.label: Check purpose
quickFacts.value: Name the uncertainty and the intended result.

quickFacts.label: Training
quickFacts.value: Apply the applicable combined bonus once.

title: Knowledge does not mean omniscience

sections.title: A witness has a position
sections.text: In this example, a civic construct guards a sealed account of a dispute. One person says a gate was opened deliberately; another says it broke during repairs. Ask what the witness actually perceived, what the record contains, and who supplied each statement. Knowing what someone said is different from knowing whether it was true. A successful examination can reveal an intact seal or an alteration without establishing every fact of the original event. Information is useful because of its scope, not because it replaces all uncertainty.

sections.title: Ask for the useful piece
sections.text: A player says, “Can I discover which account describes the hinge we found?” That question connects observation to a concrete contradiction. The table can examine the written descriptions and the damaged object. Another player might ask whether a speaker recognizes a missing tool. Those approaches can call on different practices and sources of evidence. Do not demand a generic truth roll that swallows the whole scene. A specific question helps the DM describe both what is established and what remains open to investigation.

sections.title: Keep player knowledge in its place
sections.text: You may remember that a pictured guardian appears elsewhere in the catalogue. Your character still knows what the scene, acquired knowledge, and applicable senses establish. A familiar illustration does not expose private motives, a hidden record, or the exact rules of an unfamiliar occurrence. Equally, do not pretend to forget information the character legitimately learned. Keep a brief note of the clue and how it was obtained. This makes later deduction feel like the group using its work rather than guessing the DM’s preferred answer.

sections.title: Let exceptional methods be exceptional
sections.text: If someone wants to read a memory, perceive deception, or speak with the past, inspect the actual working. State whose information it reaches, what evidence it produces, and what limitations apply. A high practice total does not silently add any of those permissions. A narrow extraordinary result can coexist with an unresolved broader question. The witness may establish which words were spoken while leaving coercion or misunderstanding for the party to examine. Resist turning an interesting method into a promise of universal certainty.

sections.title: Carry the conclusion forward
sections.text: After comparing the accounts, the party finds that both witnesses describe different gates. The dispute now concerns who moved the warning sign. Record that conclusion and choose the next lead. If the evidence instead remains mixed, decide what action is worth taking with that uncertainty. You can seek another witness, take precautions, or postpone judgment. The point of gathering knowledge is to make better choices. An answer should enter the shared situation; it need not become a demand for more checks before anyone may act.

sections.title: A conversation about what is proved
sections.text: Player: “The witness says the repairer spoke those words. Does that prove the gate was deliberately opened?” DM: “It establishes the statement it recorded. The statement’s explanation still needs evidence.” Companion: “Then I compare it to the broken hinge instead of treating the witness as an all-knowing judge.” The table has preserved a useful discovery without expanding it into omniscience. The same distinction can apply to an extraordinary record if its actual rule provides a statement rather than a guaranteed true account. Ask what the method establishes and carry that forward honestly. A limited answer can still change who the party questions next.

sections.title: The witness was facing another way
sections.text: Change the example: the witness heard the repairer but did not see the gate. That observation may support a timeline while leaving the physical event unresolved. The party can compare sounds, damage, another account, or the repair records. Do not pretend the missing view exists because the witness looks authoritative. For an exercise, explain how one clue supports two different interpretations. A broken hinge might result from deliberate force or an overloaded mechanism. Name another piece of evidence that would distinguish them. The explanation demonstrates reasoning from actual information, not extracting a preferred conclusion from a sufficiently high result.

imagePurpose: The civic witness protects testimony. Place its figure beside the comparison of a witnessed event, a recorded statement, and an interpretation; the portrait supplies no automatic truth-detection power.

quickFacts.label: Evidence
quickFacts.value: Name what was observed, recorded, or inferred.

quickFacts.label: A limit
quickFacts.value: Knowledge and training do not automatically reveal hidden thoughts.

title: Sense a location, not a whole biography

sections.title: The sound beneath the boards
sections.text: A creature moves beyond a wall, and the party hears the floor creak. In this example, ordinary hearing gives a direction and a reason to be cautious; the table must decide whether it locates the particular target accurately enough for the proposed action. A granted contact sense may establish more, within its actual scope. Do not replace that reading with the creature’s name or an assumption that all unusual senses behave alike. Ask which surface is involved, what information reaches the character, and what remains uncertain.

sections.title: Read the sense as a rule
sections.text: Vision, blindsight, tremorsense, and other authored methods can provide legitimate target location. They differ in medium, reach, conditions, and the information they convey. Read the particular grant rather than borrowing a definition from another game. The hollowbark listener’s rooted posture is a useful picture of contact with a place, but the picture cannot extend a rule through every wall or floor. Exceptional perception should be explained in a sentence another player can use: what is sensed, where, and under what conditions.

sections.title: Location is one part of targeting
sections.text: Suppose a granted sense establishes that a person stands behind the partition. That answers the location question. The working still needs its actual subject, behavior, reach, and delivery method. A projected effect can meet the partition as an obstacle; a properly granted direct manifestation follows its own targeting terms. Neither method acquires mind reading because a location is known. Keep the separate questions visible. A permission to affect a known person is not permission to know their identity, intentions, equipment, or every condition they carry.

sections.title: Ask what changed
sections.text: The target climbs from the contacted floor onto a suspended platform. The party should reassess what the sense can establish now. A remembered location may be useful evidence, but it need not remain exact after movement. Another player can watch an exit, listen, illuminate the room, or negotiate access to the space. These ordinary contributions matter because perception is situated. Avoid treating the initial successful location as a permanent lock unless the acquired rule actually provides that continuing information. The scene may now support a different plan.

sections.title: Give uncertainty a place
sections.text: If the sense does not locate the target, propose a known area or spot where an action could reasonably be attempted. Explain what success would change and what the uncertainty means. An area does not guarantee a hidden person is inside it. The DM can resolve the unknown circumstance without granting invented knowledge to the character. Write the actual sensory condition beside the working on paper. When the target changes position or the medium disappears, everyone can recognize which question must be reopened.

sections.title: A conversation about the contacted surface
sections.text: Player: “My granted sense uses contact with the floor. Can it locate someone in this room?” DM: “Read the stated medium and reach. The person on the landing is connected through the stone; the suspended platform presents another question.” Player: “Then I can target the located person with a suitable working, but I do not claim a location on the platform.” The table applies the actual grant rather than accepting or rejecting every contact sense as one package. The player can now ask a companion to observe the platform. Different methods provide complementary information without silently giving all characters the same exceptional perception.

sections.title: The exercise: say what the sense cannot reveal
sections.text: Choose one acquired sense and write a successful observation in plain language. Then identify something that observation does not establish: a motive, a private name, the contents of a sealed bag, or an unrelated event elsewhere. Explain the difference using the actual rule. A target location can be enough for a particular working without supplying a complete biography. Now change the medium or position and review the sense again. If your example assumes the answer survives every change, check whether the grant truly says so. A strong sensory permission has meaningful scope; it does not need to answer every possible question to be useful.

imagePurpose: The rooted listener illustrates a location learned through contact rather than sight. Mark the contacted surface in the composition, making the sense’s actual medium and limits visible.

quickFacts.label: Specific target
quickFacts.value: Locate it through an applicable sense.

quickFacts.label: Separate questions
quickFacts.value: Location, access, reach, and delivery each matter.

title: A hidden creature still needs a location

sections.title: A trail is not a target
sections.text: In this example, a silent cat has crossed a ruined observatory. The party finds disturbed dust and a strand of fur near a broken window. Those clues establish a passage, not a guaranteed present location. A player can follow the signs, watch the exits, or ask what cover interrupts the view. The DM need not hide every visible fact behind a check. Useful description gives players places to investigate. Keep the distinction between evidence of past movement and perception of the creature now.

sections.title: Make the search understandable
sections.text: “I look for the creature” becomes clearer when the player names a position and method. From the doorway, can they see under the desk? Will moving the lantern illuminate the balcony or reveal the searcher? Does a companion cover the stair? The table can appraise uncertainty and consequences from those details. Concealment does not always mean a special rule called invisibility, and an unusual appearance does not establish either. Read the creature’s actual abilities if an exceptional concealment effect matters to the scene.

sections.title: Preserve what the clue gives you
sections.text: A fresh sound comes from the upper landing. It might locate a creature sufficiently for a particular attempt, or it might leave only a likely region. Establish that before committing. A player may have an applicable sense that changes the answer, while another only has ordinary hearing. The group can share observations without granting each observer the same sense. Describing what you noticed lets companions choose their own legitimate methods. Information can make cooperation easier without becoming an automatic shared targeting permission.

sections.title: Aim at a known place when appropriate
sections.text: The player chooses to disturb the visible curtain rather than claim a precise unseen target behind it. This is an attempt at a known object or area. It still needs the actual working’s access and scope. The curtain may move while the creature has already left, or it may reveal someone who was there. State what the effect does to that place, not what you hope it proves. The scene’s result can provide new information, but wishing for a hidden recipient does not put one inside the area.

sections.title: Use the result, including a quiet result
sections.text: The party finds a safe route to the balcony and discovers the cat guarding an injured companion. Their next choice can be to withdraw, offer space, investigate the injury, or risk a closer approach. Successful searching need not end in attack. If nothing is found, the party still knows which places it checked and what precautions it took. Record those facts. Repeating an identical search endlessly should not replace deciding whether to widen the search, wait, or pursue a different objective.

sections.title: A conversation beside the curtain
sections.text: Player: “I think the cat is behind the curtain, so I target it there.” DM: “You have evidence it went that way, but no current location. Can your method affect the known curtain or area?” Player: “I can disturb the curtain itself. That may reveal what is there.” Companion: “I watch the side passage while you do.” The group now has a clear method and a way to use any new information. It has not assumed that the hidden creature stayed put. If the curtain moves and nothing is visible, the watched exit and earlier clues still matter to the next decision.

sections.title: The exercise: three different kinds of confidence
sections.text: Compare seeing a creature at a window, finding fresh prints near that window, and knowing that the creature usually sleeps there. The first can establish a current sensory location if the relevant conditions permit. The second is evidence of movement. The third is prior information about a habit. Neither of the latter automatically supplies a present targeting lock. Describe a useful action from each situation. Observing a known opening, following a trail, or questioning someone about the habit can all move the scene forward. The answer should preserve what is genuinely known while giving the character an intelligible way to act.

imagePurpose: The lynx’s low posture and ruined-observatory setting support a scene about tracks, concealment, and changing lines of sight. The image must not imply an unlisted invisibility power.

quickFacts.label: Past and present
quickFacts.value: A track suggests movement; it does not guarantee current location.

quickFacts.label: Known area
quickFacts.value: Selecting a place does not guarantee a hidden recipient is there.

title: A known target still needs a route

sections.title: Four questions at the doorway
sections.text: A surveyor stands across a cluttered chamber. You can see it through a narrow gap. In this example, begin with four questions: can you locate the particular target, does your acquired rule permit the intended change, does the reach cover it, and can this delivery method operate through the situation? A clear yes to sight is useful. It does not settle the other questions. Keep an obstacle in the description long enough for its practical effect to be appraised instead of letting a dramatic ability name erase it.

sections.title: Follow the projected path
sections.text: A projected working travels along an actual delivery path. Pillars, screens, people, and openings can therefore matter. The table applies the relevant authored scope and cover treatment to the proposed path. A player can seek a different angle, remove an obstacle, or ask a companion to change the scene. Do not assume that acquiring a larger range bypasses the obstruction. Range permits reach; it does not turn a projected delivery into direct manifestation or make an unknown recipient visible through everything between you.

sections.title: Read direct manifestation carefully
sections.text: A properly granted direct manifestation does not use projected cover penalties merely because an object lies between actor and target. It still needs a legitimate targeting method and the actual permission to produce its result. “I do it directly” cannot rewrite a working whose delivery was acquired differently. Ask where the effect begins, what it changes, and how that recipient is identified. An authored exception can be exciting, but its source and limits must be available to the table before someone relies on it.

sections.title: Changing position is real work
sections.text: The player moves toward a second opening while another holds the surveyor’s attention. Track the actor’s remaining movement across the whole round. Arriving at a new phase does not refill it. If the proposed move exceeds the remaining allowance, use an appropriate acquired extension or agree a contextual consequence before committing. The new angle may improve the path while exposing the mover. That is a meaningful tactical decision because both parts of the scene remain true. Movement should change circumstances, not merely repaint an attack bonus.

sections.title: Describe the final attempt
sections.text: “From this opening, I can see the surveyor’s frame and project the working through the clear gap” is a playable description. Resolve whatever meaningful uncertainty remains with the established check, defense, or agreed method. If the target moves or the screen falls, reassess the relevant part of the plan. On paper, a quick sketch of actor, obstacle, opening, and recipient is often enough. It records the shared geometry without requiring a precise tactical map for every discussion or importing another game’s cover rules.

sections.title: A conversation about the gap
sections.text: Player: “I can see the frame through the opening. My effect is projected.” DM: “Show the path from your position. The screen covers most of that line.” Player: “I move toward the second opening, using what movement remains.” Companion: “I can warn you if the surveyor turns.” The table can now appraise the actual path and any meaningful interference. This example does not guarantee that the new angle is clear or that watching grants a mechanical bonus. It keeps each contribution specific. If the player instead has a direct manifestation, read that method honestly rather than relabeling the projected effect after encountering an inconvenient screen.

sections.title: The exercise: four answers on one sketch
sections.text: Draw an actor, a located recipient, and a wall between them. Write the acquired behavior, reach, and delivery beside the drawing. Can you explain the attempt without assuming that one answer settles all the others? A visible recipient can still lie outside reach. A recipient within reach can remain unknown. A located target can be blocked from a projected trajectory while an actual direct manifestation uses different delivery terms. The sketch is successful when those distinctions are clear. It need not import precise grid movement or another game’s cover categories to make the party’s proposed method understandable.

imagePurpose: Use the surveyor’s beam geometry beside a plan of intervening surfaces. The illustration grounds delivery and obstacles without granting its abilities to the reader’s character.

quickFacts.label: Reach
quickFacts.value: Distance permission does not supply perception or a clear path.

quickFacts.label: Delivery
quickFacts.value: Use the actual projected or direct method of the working.

title: An area is a real place

sections.title: Name what occupies the space
sections.text: A damaged landing holds a worker, a rescuer, a broken stair, and loose boards. In this example, the player wants to influence an area around them. Describe the actual place before resolving the working. Which parts are inside its acquired shape? Which subjects can the rule affect? Where do its effects originate? A named area is not an abstract pile of enemies. Its contents can include companions, objects, bystanders, and empty space, each of which matters according to the actual rule.

sections.title: An area does not invent a behavior
sections.text: A player who can move existing water may arrange water through a permitted area. That permission does not automatically heal everyone within it, extinguish every kind of hazard, or distinguish friends by loyalty. Those outcomes require their actual subject and behavior. Output, reach, shape, duration, and selectivity describe different parts of an expression. Read the ingredients that establish each needed part. A larger delivery can distribute an eligible result; it cannot manufacture a missing verb or convert a harmful effect into a beneficial one.

sections.title: Ask who is meant to be affected
sections.text: The player wants to clear water around the stranded worker while leaving the support under the rescuer intact. The table examines whether this arrangement fits the actual working. If selective control is not available, a less ambitious route may solve the problem: guide a smaller flow, move the rescuer first, or use tools around the support. State the desired exclusions before commitment. A friendly character should not be secretly exempted after resolution just because the effect’s name sounded protective. The record and agreed expression determine the recipients.

sections.title: Keep each effect legible
sections.text: A capability may contain several effects, but nesting them does not silently give each a free independent action or an unrelated recipient. Explain how the declared working coheres and what each part changes. A real use may need more information than its short title. The party can still make an elegant combined plan; elegance comes from understandable dependencies. If two parts need different subjects or targeting methods, show them. If a condition ends one part, do not assume that all other consequences also disappear unless their rules say so.

sections.title: Learn from the changed space
sections.text: The player chooses to drain the landing before anyone crosses. The revealed boards show that another support is broken. This new information changes the rescue route. Alternatively, an attempted flow can leave a slippery surface or move debris toward the bank under the agreed consequences. Record the actual scene rather than only a success label. When an area working ends, ask what was temporary, what physically changed, and what still needs cleanup. The distinction makes later choices understandable without introducing a universal automatic aftermath rule.

sections.title: A conversation about the exclusion
sections.text: Player: “I want the flow to move the debris, but not the rescuer.” DM: “Which part of your actual rule provides that arrangement?” Player: “It controls existing water; it does not directly move every subject in the area. I will guide the flow away from the rope instead.” Companion: “Then I keep the worker on the dry section.” The proposed selectivity has become a concrete route rather than an automatic exemption for friends. The table still appraises the actual volume, obstacles, and risk. The example illustrates asking which part of the effect can genuinely be shaped, not requiring every area working to be hazardous.

sections.title: The exercise: recipients before results
sections.text: Sketch a small space with a companion, a bystander, an object, and the intended target. Select a working your character actually owns and state what it would change in that space. Which recipients are covered by its subject and arrangement? Which are excluded by an actual rule or practical route? Do not answer only “enemies.” Explain how the effect identifies them, if it really does. Now move the bystander and ask whether the attempt must change. The exercise teaches you to preserve the working’s actual recipients while discussing a vivid scene, rather than adding invisible exclusions after resolution because the outcome became awkward.

imagePurpose: The bridge rescue provides several recipients within one threatened space. Annotate people, structures, and water separately to show why choosing an area does not supply automatic selectivity.

quickFacts.label: Scope
quickFacts.value: Place, subject, recipients, and behavior remain distinct.

quickFacts.label: Before commitment
quickFacts.value: Name the intended exclusions and continuing terms.

title: Negotiate the consequence you mean

sections.title: Make an offer the table can examine
sections.text: In this example, a water shaper wants to hold a damaged crossing while companions evacuate a worker. Say what happens, how long help is needed, and what pressure makes the attempt demanding. The DM and player can discuss an execution consequence before the attempt is committed. It might involve Vitality, continued direction, lost access until an agreed condition, a task, or a narrative complication. Do not assume that every extraordinary use owes the same kind of payment. The interesting choice begins with understanding what is at stake.

sections.title: Separate purchase from execution
sections.text: The character already acquired the ingredients. Their BU prices describe that acquisition and were reviewed for the campaign. Execution Cost describes this use in this situation. It is not a new purchase of every nested ingredient. Conversely, offering a larger execution payment does not automatically acquire an unrelated new permission. If the player needs a different behavior, identify it honestly. The table can review a new authored ingredient or agree a clear contextual exception, rather than hiding an expanded power inside a vague promise to pay more.

sections.title: Compare two possible burdens
sections.text: The player offers to remain at the bank directing the support until everyone crosses. A companion worries that this will prevent the shaper from rescuing someone upstream. The alternative offer is a more forceful expression with a different agreed consequence. These are example negotiations, not fixed prices. Ask which option preserves the desired scene and gives the player a meaningful choice. A restriction should specify what is restricted, when it applies, and how it ends. A narrative complication should have a comprehensible relationship to the attempt.

sections.title: Agree what persistence requires
sections.text: If the working is maintained, record its continuation terms and the agreed maintenance point. Council is a useful shared point in the round rhythm. One capability’s multiple effects do not automatically become several independent upkeep tracks, while several maintained capabilities carry their respective agreed requirements. Damage-triggered additional repayment for Vitality-only upkeep remains an unresolved alpha question. Do not fill that gap with an automatic counter policy. The table can use clearly agreed continuation consequences without pretending that the pending numerical scheme is settled.

sections.title: Respect the chosen outcome
sections.text: After agreement, resolve the attempt and apply its actual result. If the player accepts a temporary loss of access, a new round does not erase it unless that was the stated ending condition. If the scene no longer needs the working, decide whether ending it avoids future maintenance and which established consequences remain. Write a brief record in plain words. The best negotiated consequence is one the player remembers and the table can administer, rather than an impressive paragraph that nobody can explain when the next choice arrives.

sections.title: A conversation about an unwanted payment
sections.text: DM: “Holding the channel under this pressure would require a continuing restriction.” Player: “I do not want to lose the working for the rest of the journey. Could I remain directing it until the crossing ends instead?” DM: “That fits this proposal if you stay in position.” Companion: “I can take the worker while you hold the route.” This is a negotiated example, not a formula for exchangeable prices. The player has identified which consequence they do not want and proposed a method that changes the pressure. The table can accept, revise, or explain why it does not fit. A meaningful offer makes the intended commitment visible before the action is resolved.

sections.title: A second scene needs a second appraisal
sections.text: Compare the same working used to move water between bowls in a calm workshop. The rescue’s urgency, people, and failing support are absent. Its exact consequence need not automatically follow every trivial use forever. Conversely, a more dangerous crossing does not guarantee the calm result simply because the capability is unchanged. Read any actual fixed cost in the rule, then appraise the contextual terms honestly. For an exercise, name one changed circumstance that would matter and explain why. More time, better support, a different recipient, or reduced scope can change the proposal without providing an unrelated new permission.

imagePurpose: The tools support two contrasting rescue methods with different practical burdens. Place the rope beside the ordinary route and the flask beside the extraordinary route, rather than illustrating Cost as damage alone.

quickFacts.label: Before use
quickFacts.value: Agree consequence, timing, scope, and ending condition.

quickFacts.label: Alpha boundary
quickFacts.value: The Vitality damage-trigger repayment scheme remains pending.

title: Keep one thing going

sections.title: The promise after the first moment
sections.text: In this example, a character keeps water away from a camp beneath a leaking ledge. The initial success is only part of the useful result. Everyone needs to know whether the working continues by itself, requires the character’s direction, has an authored duration, or depends on an ongoing consequence. These possibilities are different. A water channel dug with ordinary tools can remain after the digger walks away; a maintained arrangement may not. Describe the actual method before treating all continuing results as one universal form of concentration. A capability’s record gives the conversation its starting point.

sections.title: One coherent record
sections.text: Write the capability, the active result, its recipient or place, the next maintenance point, and the condition that ends it. Several effects inside the capability should remain legible, but they do not automatically become separate upkeep tracks simply because the record has several headings. Another maintained capability has its own agreed continuation requirements. The party needs to recognize which working they are relying on. If someone says “the shelter is protected,” ask whether that means water diverted, heat retained, a barrier held, or several actual results. A single appealing name can otherwise conceal missing terms.

sections.title: A conversation at Council
sections.text: Player: “I keep the flow outside our bedding while we prepare to move.” DM: “Your agreed continuation requires directing it at Council. Will you maintain it this round?” Player: “Yes. I stay beside the channel. Can someone carry my pack?” Companion: “I will, while I check the route.” This example uses terms the table already accepted; it does not establish a universal payment. The decision gives the other characters a concrete contribution. Council makes continuation visible before new intents depend on it, rather than leaving a silent assumption buried in yesterday’s description of the capability.

sections.title: Do not confuse ending with undoing
sections.text: When the character ends the flow, temporary control stops according to its rule. The wet ground, displaced debris, and channel already dug remain whatever the actual scene establishes. An accepted exhaustion, lost access, or other consequence uses its own ending condition; it does not vanish because the capability is no longer active. Likewise, a persistent independent result need not demand upkeep simply because it lasts. Separate the working, its physical aftermath, and the actor’s consequences. This is especially helpful when another character wants to take over an ordinary task instead of inheriting an extraordinary permission.

sections.title: The ledge breaks
sections.text: Compare a changed situation. The first camp has a narrow leak; the second suffers a collapse that sends a new stream through the shelter. The existing record has not automatically expanded to solve the new problem. Ask whether its subject, scale, place, and control still cover the proposed result. The character can maintain the original protection while companions evacuate, attempt an eligible stronger expression with newly agreed consequences, or end it and choose another method. Damage alone does not invoke a settled universal Vitality repayment policy: that alpha detail remains pending. The changed situation demands a described choice.

sections.title: A paper test before the next scene
sections.text: Cover the capability’s prose and read only your continuation note. Can another player tell what remains active, what you must do next, and when they should stop relying on it? If the note says only “upkeep,” it is incomplete. Rewrite it in ordinary words using the actual agreement. Now imagine the actor moves, rests, becomes unable to act, or chooses another intent. Read the relevant rule for each condition rather than inventing the same answer for all four. A compact record succeeds when it preserves the specific continuing promise with little effort at the table.

sections.title: Choose what deserves a reminder
sections.text: A useful continuation reminder names the next decision, not every sentence of the capability. “At Council, decide whether to keep directing the channel from this position” tells the player what to do. “Active” alone does not. If the continuing term is a resource requirement, record the real resource and timing. If it is an obligation, record its completion condition. Compare these notes with the actual rule before the next scene. The reminder should shorten the conversation while preserving the specific requirement; it must not turn distinct forms of upkeep into one invented universal bill.

imagePurpose: A camp under temporary protection makes continuation meaningful: someone keeps watch, a working supports shelter, and the others need rest. Use the scene to contrast active maintenance with a completed physical task.

quickFacts.label: Track
quickFacts.value: Working, next maintenance point, ending condition.

quickFacts.label: Keep distinct
quickFacts.value: Active control, lasting result, and lingering consequence.

title: Help changes the problem

sections.title: An objective with several useful edges
sections.text: A loading machine holds a failing freight platform above a group of workers. In this example, the party wants everyone clear before the support gives way. One person can warn the workers, another secure a line, another inspect the load, and another negotiate with the machine. These are distinct contributions toward the same outcome. The group need not make four identical attacks, and the DM need not invent a universal help bonus. Start by finding what each contribution actually changes. A character with little relevant extraordinary access may still see a route that the others have overlooked.

sections.title: Ask the other player what helps
sections.text: Offering assistance is easier when it leaves the actor a meaningful choice. Say, “Would a secured rope make your crossing possible?” or “If I talk to the keeper, can you check the support?” The answer might reveal that something else is more urgent. Do not narrate a companion’s acceptance, feeling, or success without their participation. A shared plan becomes clear when each person states their own contribution and the table understands its relationship to the objective. The group’s colorful abilities can coexist with practical observations, trust, and ordinary equipment.

sections.title: A conversation beneath the platform
sections.text: Player: “I want to bring the workers out, but I cannot hold the whole load.” Companion: “I can guide them along the clear wall. What keeps the passage open?” Third player: “I will ask the machine to lower the freight toward the empty bay.” DM: “It needs a safe destination. Show me the route you are offering.” The party now has questions to answer rather than a blanket promise of assistance. This example does not guarantee the machine’s cooperation. Its actual understanding, obligations, circumstances, and the party’s method determine how the conversation can be resolved.

sections.title: A shared goal is not shared permission
sections.text: The characters can share information, positions, and timing while retaining their own acquired rules. A companion’s ability to locate someone through a wall does not automatically grant that sense to every other actor. Carrying a character’s item does not necessarily confer its active benefits without the actual equipment conditions. Read what the proposed cooperation relies on. When a contribution makes a previously difficult task secure, the DM can acknowledge that changed situation. When uncertainty remains, resolve it intelligibly. Neither outcome needs a compulsory series of identical help checks.

sections.title: When one part fails
sections.text: Suppose the machine cannot lower the load because the bay is occupied. The evacuation route may still be useful. The line may still protect a worker who slips. The party can clear the bay, choose another destination, or change the goal to buying time. Do not erase successful contributions because the first complete plan failed. Conversely, do not claim that the completed warning also guarantees every worker escaped. Apply the actual result of each contribution. Shared objectives become more interesting when the group can see which parts worked and which changed the next decision.

sections.title: The quiet character has something to do
sections.text: Try this exercise: remove the party’s strongest extraordinary working from the example. List three useful contributions that remain. Suitable answers might include identifying the empty bay, moving bystanders, securing a line, calling a foreman, or keeping an exit clear. Their usefulness depends on the described site. Now restore the working and ask how those contributions support it. The lesson is not that everyone must perform a special role. A cooperative party offers opportunities to participate, including observation, planning, and conversation, without making a shy player compete for the most dramatic ability name.

sections.title: Compare protection and persuasion
sections.text: If the machine refuses to lower the load, a character guarding the exit can still protect workers while another seeks the keeper. If the keeper approves the change, the physical route must still be usable. Neither contribution automatically solves the other. Explain the relationship between them in a short sentence: “Your agreement lets us try lowering it; my cleared passage lets people move when it lowers.” This is a practical way to review a shared plan. It rewards different approaches without forcing the party to pretend that every useful action grants the same numerical assistance.

imagePurpose: The loading machine supports failing freight above workers. Show its load and the party’s different positions so cooperation reads as divided tasks, not a repeated bonus icon.

quickFacts.label: Objective
quickFacts.value: Say what the group wants to protect or change.

quickFacts.label: Contribution
quickFacts.value: Describe the actual situation your help changes.

title: Plan before the collision

sections.title: The scene before Council
sections.text: A rooftop challenger stands between the party and a banner that identifies a stolen shipment. In this worked example, the party wants the banner and a safe way down; defeating the challenger is one possible means. Describe the roof, its exits, loose tiles, and the challenger’s demands. Establish who can perceive whom and which extraordinary rules matter. The group should understand the objective before declaring intents. This avoids a familiar mistake: everyone starts attacking, and only later discovers that an ordinary negotiation or a different route could have served the original purpose.

sections.title: Council makes promises visible
sections.text: At Council, one player proposes distracting the challenger with a wager while another retrieves the banner and a third checks the descent.
