Discuss actual dependencies and likely consequences. Each character declares one coherent Main Intent; a longer description does not purchase several unrelated actions. Complexity comes from the work and dependencies of the attempt, not simply from how impressive it sounds. The table appraises the relevant Fast, Measured, or Heavy track. These example declarations do not establish fixed phase assignments for every conversation, climb, or extraordinary ability.

sections.title: Fast is not a fresh turn
sections.text: In this example’s agreed appraisal, the first direct exchange and preparatory movement happen in Fast. The challenger answers the wager, revealing that someone else has paid for the banner’s return. The information can affect later choices. Track any movement already spent against the character’s allowance for the entire round. Fast does not provide a new independent allowance or erase a continuing consequence. Nor must every participant manufacture a separate Fast action. A character whose intent depends on later work remains part of the shared scene while earlier results establish what happens next.

sections.title: Measured and Heavy follow the situation
sections.text: The banner retriever’s attempt resolves in Measured under the table’s appraisal, while the more involved work securing a descent resolves in Heavy. If the earlier exchange persuaded the challenger to permit retrieval, the Measured situation differs from the one first feared. If the challenger cuts off the route, the group must acknowledge that interference instead of completing a script unchanged. Apply the actual agreed resolution to each attempt. Tracks organize dependencies and shared timing; they are not a promise that every declared outcome occurs regardless of the scene around it.

sections.title: A conversation when the plan changes
sections.text: DM: “The challenger offers the banner if you recover the cargo from below.” Player: “My intent was to distract them while we took it. Can I accept instead?” Companion: “I can still finish the line; we may need it for the cargo.” The table can clarify the revised situation and commitments. This does not establish a universal free-intent replacement rule. It shows why declarations should be understandable enough to discuss interference and changed agreements. Do not treat improvisation as secretly obtaining several additional actions, or treat a reasonable clarification as grounds to ignore the fiction.

sections.title: What the next Council needs
sections.text: After Heavy, record where everyone is, which intents resolved, remaining consequences, active workings, and the banner’s actual status. Begin the next Council from that result. Reaction availability and round movement follow their proper refresh timing; lasting restrictions keep their stated conditions. A short recap can be spoken: “We have the banner, the challenger wants help, and the descent line is ready.” If the party did not secure the banner, say that just as clearly. The rhythm becomes useful when it carries a changed situation forward, without requiring initiative rolls or four separate personal turns per character.

sections.title: The exercise: one intent through the rhythm
sections.text: Write one objective for the rooftop scene, then describe the dependencies needed to pursue it. Ask the table to appraise their placement in the rhythm. Do not fill four boxes with four unrelated actions merely because there are four named phases. In the example, retrieving the banner can depend on a permitted approach and a safe route away; those details help explain timing and interference. The answer should preserve the coherent goal while showing what an earlier result can change. If your description contains another independent objective, identify it openly rather than hiding it as a decorative clause.

imagePurpose: The rooftop challenger anchors a round about positioning, a contested banner, and a route to safety. The art should show ledges and a shared objective rather than present a static combat portrait.

quickFacts.label: Rhythm
quickFacts.value: Council → Fast → Measured → Heavy.

quickFacts.label: Declaration
quickFacts.value: One coherent Main Intent, with actual dependencies.

title: Spend the reaction on an opportunity

sections.title: An interruption you can describe
sections.text: A companion’s foothold breaks above a canal. In this example, another character wants to respond before the fall carries them out of reach. A reaction begins with a perceived opportunity or threat and an intelligible immediate response. “I react” alone does not explain the attempt. Say what the actor notices, what they do, and which actual method makes it possible. The winged medic in the illustration evokes a rescue, but its presence is not a general permission for every character to fly, stop a fall, or heal someone at a distance.

sections.title: The slot is not the ability
sections.text: A character’s independent Reaction Slot permits reactive participation under the rhythm. It does not supply the ingredients of an extraordinary result. Grabbing an available line, warning someone, and producing a special descent effect rely on different circumstances or permissions. Read the actual working and its immediate scope. A reaction also needs to fit the event the actor can perceive. Knowing afterwards that a companion fell is different from being positioned and aware enough to intervene. Establish those details before resolving success instead of turning the slot into an unlimited exception to every access rule.

sections.title: A short table exchange
sections.text: Player: “I see the tile break. I throw the end of the rope I am holding.” DM: “The line can reach that position. You are trying to give them something to catch before they fall past it.” Companion: “I reach for it.” The table now has a concrete shared attempt and can resolve meaningful uncertainty. A different player might propose an acquired descent working with its own scope and consequences. These are alternative methods, not two automatic successes. The receiving character’s actual position and capacity remain part of the scene rather than a guarantee hidden inside the rescue’s name.

sections.title: Keep the rest of the round honest
sections.text: Mark the Reaction Slot when it is spent. It refreshes at Council, not whenever another dramatic event occurs or a new track begins. Movement used in the reaction still belongs to the round’s ordinary movement allowance unless an actual rule provides otherwise. A declared Main Intent and a reactive opportunity can interact; appraise their real dependencies and interference at the table. Do not quietly finish an impossible earlier plan merely because its card remains on the sheet. Reacting can create a useful tradeoff without demanding an invented universal cancellation rule.

sections.title: Now the actor cannot see the fall
sections.text: Change the example: the rescuer is inside a workshop and hears a crash but cannot identify the falling person’s location. The character may shout a warning, move to see, or act on a known place with an appropriate method. They cannot simply claim the same precise rescue as before unless an applicable sense or actual working establishes it. Compare another change: the rope was already secured around a support. That preparation may protect the falling person without requiring the same new reaction. The actual scene determines which opportunity exists.

sections.title: An exercise in immediate scope
sections.text: Which proposal is clearest: stop the fall, erase every injury the companion has, or toss the available line? The last already names an ordinary method. The first can become clear by naming a suitable acquired working and its exact recipient. The second combines a rescue with a broader unrelated promise unless the character genuinely has the relevant scope. The answer is not that reactions must be mundane or small. A remarkable response can be valid; it needs a perceived trigger, legitimate access, an intelligible immediate purpose, and an actual remaining opportunity to matter.

sections.title: Check immediate scope before the roll
sections.text: The normal reactive scope is an immediate Complexity 0–1 response affecting self/touch or one target. Read it alongside any actual granted exception. An elaborate sequence that first locates a hidden person, constructs a route, moves the whole party, and heals several recipients should not be compressed into an ordinary reaction because the moment is urgent. Separate what is immediately possible from what requires a new intent or further work. The rescue can still be remarkable; its immediate purpose, available slot, trigger, access, and eligible scope must be intelligible before the resolution is chosen.

imagePurpose: The flying rescuer supports an example of responding to a perceived fall. Compose it near the ledge and rope so the reader sees the opportunity and the limits of reach.

quickFacts.label: Availability
quickFacts.value: One independent Reaction Slot per round; refresh at Council.

quickFacts.label: Access
quickFacts.value: The slot does not provide the extraordinary working itself.

title: A failed plan can leave a better question

sections.title: Apply the agreed result
sections.text: In this worked example, the party tries to reach a stranded worker across a damaged stair. The table has agreed that a failed crossing could break a loose section while a secured line protects the rescuer from an immediate uncontrolled fall. After resolution, the stair gives way and the line catches. The worker remains stranded. These facts are the new scene. Do not compress them into “nothing happens” or quietly convert them into a different penalty after the roll. The consequence should make sense in relation to the described method and the earlier agreement.

sections.title: Keep the useful work
sections.text: The line was secured before the crossing and remains attached under this example’s circumstances. A companion has already identified a sound post, and the warning has brought help to the bank. Those contributions do not vanish merely because the final objective was not yet achieved. Equally, preparation does not guarantee every later task. The rope can be damaged, a post can fail, or someone can remain beyond reach if the actual result establishes that. Record what is true now. Specific aftermath gives players more to work with than a single success-or-failure label.

sections.title: A conversation from the line
sections.text: Player: “I am hanging below the landing. Can I see the window on its underside?” DM: “Yes. The broken stair has exposed it.” Companion: “I can hold the line while you ask the worker to open it.” Player: “Then I try to reach that opening.” This exchange does not refund resources or guarantee the new attempt. It follows a changed route that the first plan revealed. The party can appraise reach, support, uncertainty, and consequences again. Their next decision is different because the earlier result changed the place, not because they asked to roll the same sentence until it worked.

sections.title: When repetition really is a choice
sections.text: Some tasks allow another attempt: time passes, the method is adjusted, the obstacle remains, and the consequences of trying again are understood. Other results remove the opportunity, reveal that the method cannot work, or demand a different approach. Ask which situation applies. A failed effort to persuade someone may leave new information or damaged trust rather than an unlimited invitation to repeat the same demand. A failed search can narrow the places checked. A broken stair cannot be treated as intact on the next roll just because the character has a favorable total.

sections.title: Use ambition without hiding a new power
sections.text: The player now proposes shaping water to lift the rescuer toward the exposed window. Check the actual subject and behavior rather than declaring that failure permits anything cinematic. The Rule of Cool supports discussing an engaging response. If the existing permission fits, appraise this expression and its consequences. If it does not, say what is missing and consider an ordinary route or an explicit contextual agreement. A new consequence may support greater eligible effort; it does not silently buy unrelated access. The scene stays imaginative when those boundaries are understandable.

sections.title: The exercise: write an aftermath
sections.text: Choose a task from your own character: negotiating safe passage, repairing a gate, climbing a wall, or locating a missing object. Write a plausible result in which the goal is not achieved but something changes usefully. Then write the next question that result invites. An explanation such as “the gate stays closed, but we discover the hinge was replaced yesterday; who supplied it?” is stronger than “try again.” The answer need not always be favorable. It should be specific enough to carry consequences and decisions forward, with the player still able to understand the shared situation.

sections.title: A partial result is a specific result
sections.text: A table may agree that an attempt can produce an intermediate outcome, but the phrase “partial success” is not enough by itself. Say what changed: the worker reaches the landing but the supplies remain above, the stair is braced only while someone holds it, or the route is revealed without being secured. Record the actual consequence and any continuing requirement. The new scene should give the players a meaningful next choice. Do not use an appealing label to conceal an invented result that contradicts the method or the stakes everyone accepted.

imagePurpose: Return to the bridge from a lower viewpoint, emphasizing a caught rope and newly exposed route. The changed composition should make the useful aftermath of failure visible.

quickFacts.label: After resolution
quickFacts.value: Record the actual position, resources, information, and consequences.

quickFacts.label: Next question
quickFacts.value: Choose from the changed scene; do not erase it.

title: Cross without winning a fight

sections.title: Name the goal in the place
sections.text: A herd blocks the safest ford. In this example, the party needs to reach a settlement before supplies run short. Their goal is crossing, not necessarily killing the animals. Ask about the banks, currents, herd movement, young animals, and other possible routes. The DM can describe evident behavior. Players can watch, wait, communicate, distract, guide, or alter their own route according to the actual circumstances and permissions. A creature’s BU and combat record help when those mechanics matter; they do not turn every encounter into a challenge that must end with its defeat.

sections.title: Look for what the other side protects
sections.text: The grazers keep returning toward their young and leave a narrow retreat route behind them. That observation suggests a useful approach: give them space rather than crowd the vulnerable part of the herd. It does not grant automatic animal obedience or a universal bonus. The group still needs a method that works in this place. A player with applicable knowledge may interpret behavior; another can inspect the water; another can ensure nobody approaches from behind. Meaningful uncertainty can be resolved with the appropriate practice or other agreed method after the intended contribution is clear.

sections.title: A conversation on the bank
sections.text: Player: “We want to cross without separating the young. Can we wait until the adults move?” DM: “They are unsettled because your carts block their route back to the meadow.” Companion: “I move our lead cart away from that path.” Player: “Then I watch for the gap they leave.” These ordinary decisions alter the situation without inventing a new power. The herd may settle or the passage may remain risky under the actual result. The conversation works because the party respects an observable purpose and describes practical changes, rather than demanding an undefined roll to make the animals friendly.

sections.title: Exceptional solutions have actual subjects
sections.text: A character might offer a suitable working to redirect water, produce a harmless distraction, or communicate in a granted way. Read exactly what it permits. Owning a broad-sounding nature theme does not automatically command every living creature or rewrite its motives. A distraction can attract attention without controlling what the animal does next. A route shaped through the water still needs to accommodate the people and supplies using it. If the effect involves recipients or a continuing result, establish those terms before companions depend on it. Useful extraordinary access often supports an ordinary plan.

sections.title: Compare the night crossing
sections.text: Now change the situation: darkness obscures the far bank and the current has risen. Waiting for the same opening may no longer be enough. The group needs legitimate perception of the route, a sound means of crossing, and a plan for the supplies. A clever daytime solution should not erase new uncertainty. Nor does the changed scene require a fight. The party might shelter, investigate another route, seek local guidance, or negotiate consequences for a demanding attempt. Compare those options against the objective and what the characters actually know, not a compulsory difficulty label.

sections.title: What counts as progress
sections.text: The party crosses only the essential medicine and sends someone to find help for the remaining carts. They have not completed the entire journey, but the most urgent need is served. Record who crossed, what remains, and which obligations follow. Other groups might safely wait and lose time, or find a longer route. These can all be meaningful outcomes. For a practice exercise, state the ford scene without mentioning attacks. List three outcomes the party would welcome and one consequence it would accept. That list gives the table more useful directions than a single instruction to clear the encounter.

sections.title: Take the creatures out of the exercise
sections.text: Imagine the same ford obstructed by fallen timber instead of a herd. Observation, route selection, cargo handling, time, and the party’s actual access still matter. Now restore the animals and name what changes: motives, movement, young to protect, and possible responses to the party. This comparison helps distinguish a living encounter from a static barrier. The answer should not reduce animals to obedient obstacles or compulsory opponents. A useful encounter gives the party a purpose in a place and lets the creatures’ actual behavior affect how that purpose can be pursued.

imagePurpose: The herd at the ford illustrates space, young animals, and a retreat route. Use a wider scene or annotated crop to teach passage and observation rather than presenting a creature as a compulsory enemy.

quickFacts.label: Objective
quickFacts.value: Passage, safety, time, or supplies can matter more than defeat.

quickFacts.label: Observation
quickFacts.value: Use the creature’s actual behavior and the place around it.

title: Follow evidence through a place

sections.title: A question the site can answer
sections.text: Someone has altered a warning on a ruined crossing. In this example, a monument attendant remembers repairs and visitors within its actual capabilities. The party wants to know which warning travelers would have seen. Start with that question. The stone, its position, damaged lettering, and nearby tracks may all contain evidence. A mystery becomes easier to investigate when players can name what they are looking for and what a discovery would change. They need not guess the title of a hidden clue or make a generic investigation roll before the place becomes available.

sections.title: Observation before interpretation
sections.text: A character notices fresh cuts beneath old weathering. That observation differs from concluding who made them or why. Another recognizes a mason’s mark; another compares the warning to a traveler’s account. Keep those contributions distinct. The DM can establish evident details directly and resolve meaningful uncertainty where it remains. A known clue should not disappear because another character fails a different check. Write it in plain language with its source: “Fresh marks under the replaced warning, observed at the crossing.” This small habit keeps the group’s later reasoning anchored in information it actually has.

sections.title: The attendant knows something particular
sections.text: Ask the attendant what it can genuinely recall or perceive. Its age and carved appearance are evocative, but neither grants complete access to every historical event. If the party uses an extraordinary working to read a trace, inspect the actual subject, behavior, scope, and available information. A record of a repair might identify a visitor without revealing their motive. Treat that boundary as an invitation to another lead. Narrow information is valuable when it answers a clear question; it does not need to solve the whole story to justify the method.

sections.title: A conversation over the lettering
sections.text: Player: “Can the attendant tell whether the warning changed before the last caravan passed?” DM: “It remembers the repair, but not every departure. What can you compare?” Companion: “The caravan gave us a copied inscription. I put it beside the stone.” Player: “Then we can establish whether they saw the old wording.” This exchange combines a witness and an ordinary object. The comparison can be secure or uncertain according to the actual records. The players are not promised that a successful check makes their favorite suspect guilty. They are making the next decision better informed.

sections.title: Two routes from the same discovery
sections.text: The copied warning differs from the stone. One group follows the mason’s mark toward a workshop. Another goes to the caravan to warn it about the route. Both use the discovery, but they serve different priorities. The first seeks responsibility; the second protects travelers. A scene should let those priorities matter. The DM can describe what each route costs in time, exposure, or obligation without inventing a fixed penalty. A player should know the likely tradeoff before choosing. Information opens decisions; it should not always funnel every party into the same next roll.

sections.title: When the record is incomplete
sections.text: Change the example: the copied inscription is torn, and the attendant’s account stops before the repair finished. The group can still establish some facts while leaving others unknown. Ask which conclusion is supported and which needs more evidence. A character may choose precautions without certainty. Protecting the caravan does not require first proving a suspect’s motive. Avoid filling a gap with an unlisted supernatural ability or declaring that nothing can be done until the entire mystery is solved. Partial knowledge can be enough to justify a useful and consequential next step.

sections.title: The exercise: three lines of evidence
sections.text: Choose a familiar place from your campaign and write an observation, an interpretation, and a next question. For the crossing: “new cuts below old weathering”; “the warning may have been altered after installation”; “who worked here since the caravan left?” The explanation matters: the interpretation follows from a clue but is not identical to it. A different cause might fit. Your next question tests that uncertainty instead of merely restating suspicion. Keep the three lines with the party notes. They make discussion accessible to someone who missed the original scene and help prevent a remembered theory becoming a false established fact.

imagePurpose: The monument attendant and a marked stone support a scene about repairs, visitors, and trace evidence. Compose the portrait beside a sequence of three material clues; the art must not imply universal access to the past.

quickFacts.label: Record
quickFacts.value: Observation, source, interpretation, next question.

quickFacts.label: Scope
quickFacts.value: An extraordinary trace gives the information its rule establishes.

title: A bargain is not control

sections.title: Say what you are offering
sections.text: A lesser contract spirit disputes a promise that keeps a workshop closed. In this example, the party wants access to a trapped courier without destroying evidence of the agreement. Ask what the spirit claims, what the written terms say, and who is able to change them. A player can offer a new arrangement, uncover a misunderstanding, or challenge an interpretation. This is a negotiation with a purpose. “I roll Influence” does not yet describe what the other side is being asked to accept or why acceptance would make sense to it.

sections.title: Give the other side a reason
sections.text: A credible offer connects to something the other party values. The courier can preserve the damaged document, the workshop owner can complete an unfinished delivery, or the group can investigate who replaced a seal. These are example offers, not universal prices. Ask what each side can actually promise. A player cannot guarantee a distant official’s decision without the means to secure it. The spirit need not accept simply because a character has a strong bonus. Applicable resolution addresses meaningful uncertainty in an intelligible attempt, while the actual situation and scope remain relevant.

sections.title: Words need shared meanings
sections.text: Before committing to an unusual bargain, clarify the important terms in plain language. Does access mean entering the room, taking the courier away, or removing every protected object? Who must perform the promised task, and when is the obligation fulfilled? This supports a fair dramatic agreement rather than a puzzle built from unstated vocabulary. If a spirit is deliberately literal, make that behavior part of the scene. Players can enjoy careful wording without being expected to foresee a secret definition for every ordinary word. A consequence should be understandable enough to choose.

sections.title: A conversation about the seal
sections.text: Player: “We will preserve your record while we take the courier to safety.” DM: “The spirit says removing the courier breaks the named obligation. It will permit a witness to examine the changed seal.” Companion: “Then I ask to inspect it here, with the courier present.” The goal has shifted from immediate extraction toward testing the claim. This is not automatically a failed scene. The offer has revealed a useful boundary. The party can proceed, seek another route, or accept a different obligation after its terms are clear. A character’s personality can shape the offer without replacing its actual content.

sections.title: Influence does not erase another person
sections.text: An ordinary social check is not a universal command over someone’s choices, and it should not dictate another player character’s feelings without that player’s participation. Extraordinary compulsion needs its actual acquired rule, recipient, reach, and limits. A title such as commanding presence cannot provide every such outcome. Even a valid supernatural result should be applied according to what it really changes. If it causes one permitted response, do not silently expand that into lifelong loyalty, shared beliefs, or permission to rewrite all later decisions. Keep the character’s actual access visible.

sections.title: Compare the promise you cannot keep
sections.text: Now the party proposes retrieving a missing object but knows that it has already been destroyed. That changes the truth and risk of the offer. They may negotiate a substitute, reveal the loss, or make a deceptive attempt with intelligible stakes. The DM should not treat all three methods as identical. A successful lie can change what someone believes without making the promised object exist. The party’s future obligation and the possibility of discovery remain whatever the actual result establishes. Social play becomes useful when its consequences continue into later decisions.

sections.title: Leave with a playable agreement
sections.text: Write the final agreement as a short record: the parties, allowed action, obligation, completion condition, and any retained uncertainty. Read it aloud so everyone can correct a misunderstanding. This is especially important when the promise restricts a character’s access or creates a continuing consequence. For an exercise, remove all dramatic titles from the contract scene and explain what each party wants. If the bargain still makes sense, the scene has a strong foundation. If it becomes meaningless, clarify the actual interests before adding more elaborate language or extraordinary effects.

imagePurpose: The disputed-contract spirit illustrates words with consequences. Put the document and opposing parties in the composition, making terms and obligations the subject of the spread.

quickFacts.label: Offer
quickFacts.value: Ask for a specific change and give a credible reason.

quickFacts.label: Agreement
quickFacts.value: Record the parties, scope, obligation, and ending condition.

title: Make travel a shared choice

sections.title: Why this route matters
sections.text: A messenger carries a replacement part toward a settlement whose gate is failing. In this example, the party can take a narrow direct route, a safer long road, or a ferry whose operator must be found. Each choice should be described in terms the characters can understand. They may know the road’s condition, have a map, or need more information. There is no need to import a mandatory travel sequence or fixed daily encounter count. Begin with the journey’s purpose and the uncertainty that makes choosing a route interesting.

sections.title: Divide the questions, not the spotlight
sections.text: One character asks about terrain, another about supplies, another about people who know the road, and another about the messenger’s deadline. These contributions may use practices, ordinary conversation, or actual extraordinary methods. They need not become separate obligatory rolls every time the party moves. Ask what information is already established and which remaining uncertainty affects the choice. A practical contribution can be as small as noticing that the load will not fit through a passage. Make room for players who prefer a short useful statement instead of a long performance.

sections.title: A conversation over the map
sections.text: Player: “The direct route saves time, but can the cart cross its bridge?” DM: “Your map marks a foot crossing. The courier has only used it without a cart.” Companion: “We can carry the essential part and send the cart around with help.” Player: “Then our problem is protecting the smaller load, not widening the bridge.” This example changes the method without inventing an ability. The group should still establish what is carried, who takes which route, and how they will reconnect. Splitting tasks can create new responsibilities rather than automatically solving every logistical concern.

sections.title: Extraordinary travel is an actual working
sections.text: If a character proposes flight, rapid movement, a shaped path, or another exceptional method, inspect the real recipients and scope. Carrying the actor does not necessarily carry an entire party, cart, and cargo. A sustained route may need continuing direction or agreed maintenance. An extended range does not automatically locate a distant safe destination. Ask what the character knows about the place and what the method actually requires. A clear ability can make travel wonderfully different without becoming an unlimited answer to every obstacle and every hidden destination.

sections.title: Keep the cargo in the story
sections.text: The replacement part is not merely a quest label. Who holds it? Is it fragile, bulky, protected from water, or visible to people seeking it? Record its actual Load and any rule that matters. Item BU is not ordinary purchase price, and a narrative value does not create a mechanical power. The courier can explain how the part fits the gate without granting the party every workshop skill. Treat the object and its delivery as real circumstances. A safe crossing that abandons the cargo may not serve the journey’s purpose.

sections.title: Compare a changed forecast
sections.text: Now the party hears that the ferry has stopped because of rising water. The previous route choice can be reconsidered using new information. A character may investigate, negotiate assistance, reduce the load, or accept a delay. The DM can explain the likely consequence of waiting without imposing an unannounced fixed deadline penalty. If urgency is part of the agreement, keep it visible. The players should not be punished for lacking information their characters could reasonably obtain. A journey works well when preparation and new observations both affect the decisions that follow.

sections.title: What you bring into the next scene
sections.text: At arrival, note the cargo’s condition, people separated from the party, promises made along the road, and resources genuinely consumed. These facts can make the settlement scene richer. For an exercise, describe the same journey from three priorities: fastest arrival, lowest exposure, and preserving every supply. None is automatically correct. Explain which route serves each priority and what it risks under the known circumstances. This helps players recognize that travel choices belong to their characters’ values as well as their strongest numbers. A successful arrival can still leave an interesting obligation to fulfill.

imagePurpose: The urgent workshop courier supports route choices, information carried between settlements, and the need to protect a delivery. Place it with a map and visible cargo rather than a generic wilderness backdrop.

quickFacts.label: Planning
quickFacts.value: Purpose, known route, load, timing, and reconnection.

quickFacts.label: Scope
quickFacts.value: Exceptional movement affects the recipients its rule actually covers.

title: Carry the things you actually have

sections.title: A caravan asks a practical question
sections.text: A damaged axle stops a caravan outside shelter. In this example, a repair automaton can help according to its actual record, but the party still needs to know which parts and tools are available. Start with the object’s condition and the desired result. Is the plan to repair it, support it until help arrives, transfer the cargo, or continue on foot? Each method asks different questions. Owning an impressive item does not prove it contains every tool, while ordinary equipment can solve a problem without extraordinary ingredients.

sections.title: Carried is not equipped
sections.text: The equipment record distinguishes what is carried from what is currently in use. Equipped items contribute their actual active rules and slot requirements; carried unequipped objects still contribute Load. A tool can remain available to retrieve without already providing every equipped benefit. The default uses six universal equipped slots, with ordinary items using one and two-handed items two unless an actual rule establishes something else. A particular permitted item can require more, and primitives can extend the available slots. Size alone does not multiply every requirement. Read the final authored record instead of inferring it from the illustration.

sections.title: Three figures, three questions
sections.text: Item BU accounts for the mechanics acquired through equipment. Ordinary value concerns trade or the campaign’s economy. Load measures carried burden. These figures can differ greatly: a mundane component may be valuable and awkward without granting an extraordinary rule, while a small device may contain important mechanics. Keep them in separate columns. Moving equipment between characters changes who carries and can use it under its actual terms; it does not erase its existence. A backpack organizes the load but does not automatically increase capacity or make its contents disappear from the record.

sections.title: A conversation beside the wheel
sections.text: Player: “I have the brace in my pack. I take it out and support the axle.” Companion: “I can hold the cart while the patchwright works.” DM: “The support gives it a stable place to repair, but the damaged pin must still be replaced.” Player: “Do we have a spare, or can we salvage one from the empty wagon?” The discussion stays concrete. The brace changes the task; it is not a universal repair bonus. The automaton’s actual capacity and the available materials determine which part of the proposed result is possible.

sections.title: An extraordinary item has actual conditions
sections.text: If the brace carries a capability, read what activates it, who receives the result, and whether equipping or another condition is required. The item’s subject and behavior do not become the wielder’s owned positive foundation permissions merely because it is in their pack. An item may provide a granted use under its own rule while the character’s acquisition ledger remains distinct. Apply its actual stacking treatment. Two references to the same item benefit in different notes are not two separate equipped objects. A short readable item card should preserve these distinctions rather than only advertise a powerful name.

sections.title: Compare leaving the cart behind
sections.text: The party decides to carry the medicine and abandon the broken cart temporarily. Recalculate the actual carried burden and record what remains at the site. The empty cart’s condition can matter when they return. If someone carries another character’s equipment, make that transfer clear instead of granting both characters simultaneous possession. The group can share objects efficiently, but its record should follow the shared fiction. Any encumbrance consequences use the actual capacity and agreed treatment. A logistical choice should be understandable before the party commits, not an unexplained penalty discovered much later.

sections.title: The exercise: inspect one item
sections.text: Choose an item your character often uses. Write what it is, who currently holds it, whether it is equipped, its final slot requirement, Load, Item BU, and actual granted rules. Then imagine lending it to a companion. Which entries change, and which remain properties of the object? The holder and equipped state can change; the object’s authored mechanics do not automatically rewrite themselves. This exercise is useful even for a mundane rope. A reliable small inventory lets tools enter play naturally, without turning every practical task into a search through decorative descriptions.

imagePurpose: The caravan repairer supports a task with spare parts, tools, carried supplies, and equipment actively in use. Show hands and objects clearly; do not turn the art into a list of free mechanical benefits.

quickFacts.label: Record
quickFacts.value: Holder, carried/equipped state, Load, slots, Item BU, actual rules.

quickFacts.label: Default slots
quickFacts.value: Six universal slots; ordinary one, two-handed two, with explicit exceptions.

title: Rest is recovery you agree

sections.title: A pause in a real place
sections.text: The party reaches a sheltered ledge after the crossing. In this example, someone needs recovery, someone watches the route, and the group still has a delivery to finish. Ask what kind of rest the circumstances support. A short rest is a meaningful pause; a long rest is overnight sleep or equivalent recovery, not a compulsory eight-hour timer. DM and players agree whether the effects apply. Simply announcing a duration does not make danger, discomfort, or continuing obligations irrelevant. The useful question is what recovery this actual pause earns.

sections.title: Only the points restored are spent
sections.text: Short rests share a finite recovery allowance between completed long rests. Its normal amount is half maximum Vitality, rounded upward. Only actual Vitality restored consumes that allowance. In the worked example, maximum Vitality is 13, so the allowance is 7. The character begins the pause at 10/13. Restoring 3 reaches the maximum and leaves 4 for later agreed short rests. The unused points are not discarded because the character became full. Nor are they extra Vitality stored above the maximum. They remain available recovery, recorded separately from current Vitality.

sections.title: A conversation at the shelter
sections.text: Player: “I need only three points to reach my maximum. I record four short-rest recovery left.” DM: “The ledge is sheltered enough for the agreed pause, while your companion watches.” Companion: “I will keep an eye on the stair, then we can switch.” The example establishes a particular recovery agreement; it does not say every lookout arrangement guarantees rest. If continuing a working prevents the actor from resting under its actual requirements, discuss that openly. Another person can help with ordinary shelter or watch without automatically inheriting the actor’s extraordinary maintenance.

sections.title: The second pause uses the same allowance
sections.text: After later damage, the character is at 9/13. A second agreed short rest can restore the remaining 4 and reach 13/13, leaving no short-rest recovery in the pool. A third short rest does not automatically create a new allowance. It can still be a useful pause for conversation, preparation, or other agreed purposes. A table adjustment remains available, but should be explicit. The normal rule tracks actual recovery across the interval, rather than granting a fresh half-maximum heal whenever someone says they rest again.

sections.title: Long rest has its own recovery
sections.text: A completed long rest normally restores Vitality to the maximum and refreshes the short-rest allowance. Its healing is not charged against the old short-rest pool. Poor sleep or difficult conditions can support a table-agreed partial result. Establish the amount and meaning clearly, applying ordinary upward rounding when a chosen calculation needs it. Do not surprise a player with a secret adjustment after the fact. The completed long rest and its recovery terms are the relevant event; elapsed hours alone do not settle the agreement. Record the resulting current Vitality and refreshed allowance separately.

sections.title: What rest does not silently erase
sections.text: A ruined map remains ruined. A lost-access consequence may require a task. An injury may have its own recovery condition. Healing Vitality does not automatically satisfy any of those rules. Read what remains and ask which practical help is available. The party might seek a workshop, make an apology, or arrange assisted recovery. If someone is actively dying, rescue comes before treating a pause as ordinary rest. A stabilized person can recover through assisted rest under the appropriate circumstances, but stabilization itself supplies neither healing nor consciousness.

sections.title: The exercise: three honest entries
sections.text: On paper, keep current/maximum Vitality, short-rest allowance remaining, and lasting consequences on separate lines. For the worked example, begin with 10/13 and allowance 7; after the first pause write 13/13 and allowance 4. After the later injury write 9/13 and allowance 4; after recovery write 13/13 and allowance 0. Explain the entries aloud. The important distinction is between a present resource and permission to recover it later. At the next agreed completed long rest, update recovery according to that agreement and refresh the normal allowance without charging its healing to the exhausted short-rest pool.

imagePurpose: The camp should show the conditions of rest: shelter, watch, bedding, and companions helping one another. Pair it with an actual-used recovery ledger, rather than portraying elapsed time as automatic healing.

quickFacts.label: Short rest
quickFacts.value: Spend only actual Vitality restored; carry unused allowance.

quickFacts.label: Long rest
quickFacts.value: Agreed overnight recovery; healing is independent of the short-rest pool.

title: Rescue before bookkeeping

sections.title: Begin with the danger
sections.text: A companion collapses on a broken landing. In this worked example, the party must reach them while keeping the landing from failing further. At zero Vitality, collapse leaves the character unconscious and incapacitated under the normal rule. The DM establishes contextual rescue stakes. Do not assume a guaranteed sequence of safe rounds while everyone searches a sheet. Ask where the person is, what immediate hazard remains, who can reach them, and what an assisting character can actually do. A short description of those facts makes the next decision clearer than announcing only a resource value.

sections.title: Divide the urgent work
sections.text: One companion can protect a route, another can keep an attacker away, another can reach the injured person, and another can attempt stabilization. These are related but different results. Moving someone out of water can remove an immediate hazard without automatically restoring Vitality or halting every dying consequence. Successful stabilization stops the rescue countdown, but it does not heal or wake the character. Actual healing above zero ends the dying state and restores consciousness unless another consequence prevents it. The group should know which result it is attempting before resolving the action.

sections.title: A conversation on the landing
sections.text: Player: “I cross the secure section and try to stabilize them.” DM: “The broken rail leaves a clear route if the support holds. What are the others doing?” Companion: “I keep the line taut so they can work safely.” Third player: “I watch the upper doorway.” The table appraises the actual Fieldcraft attempt or a suitable creative use of owned primitives, its timing, uncertainty, and Cost. There is no universal stabilization DC to invent here. The example shows ordinary help making the rescue intelligible, while leaving each attempt’s real resolution to the table.

sections.title: Healing still needs the actual working
sections.text: A player who can control water or produce an output die does not automatically gain healing. A rescuer using an extraordinary method must have the subject and behavior that establish that result, as well as legitimate targeting and reach. A restorative name on an item should be read just as carefully. The illustrated guardian’s abilities remain its own actual record. If the character lacks suitable healing access, stabilization and practical protection can still be valuable. Do not dismiss those methods simply because they do not immediately refill the injured person’s Vitality.

sections.title: Compare an assisted recovery
sections.text: After stabilization, the party takes the companion to shelter. They can arrange assisted rest under the agreed recovery rules. That differs from attempting to rest while someone remains actively dying. Establish what the stabilized person needs, what consequences persist, and which recovery the circumstances support. Restoring Vitality may wake them while another injury still limits movement. A safe room may remove exposure while leaving an access restriction unchanged. Read those terms separately. This makes recovery a sequence of understandable conditions rather than a single word that silently solves every possible harm.

sections.title: Do not hide an outright lethal result
sections.text: The massive-damage rule and explicitly established lethal stakes remain relevant. A sheet that displays zero cannot be used to ignore a lethal overrun in the resolved damage. The contextual opportunity to rescue a collapsed character does not reverse an outright lethal result. Establish such stakes before resolution and apply the actual final damage after relevant defenses. This distinction belongs in preparation for dangerous play, not as a surprise discovered when a player asks for help. The table can discuss desired tone and boundaries while retaining the system’s real consequences.

sections.title: The exercise: what changed?
sections.text: Read these four results separately: the injured person is moved away from the edge; stabilization succeeds; healing raises Vitality above zero; an agreed completed rest restores further Vitality. Explain each result without substituting one for another. Moving changes location and immediate exposure. Stabilization halts the rescue countdown. Healing can end the dying state and restore consciousness, subject to other consequences. Rest uses its agreed recovery and allowance rules. The answer preserves the rescue’s actual stages. A party that can state them plainly is better equipped to coordinate help without wasting the scene on confused resource bookkeeping.

imagePurpose: The restoration guardian illustrates protection of an injured explorer. Compose the explorer, immediate hazard, and assisting companions so the reader sees distinct rescue tasks rather than a generic healer portrait.

quickFacts.label: Stabilization
quickFacts.value: Stops the rescue countdown; does not automatically heal or wake.

quickFacts.label: Healing
quickFacts.value: Above zero ends dying and restores consciousness unless another consequence prevents it.

title: Grow from the scene you remember

sections.title: A reason to learn something
sections.text: A character returns from the bridge rescue remembering a limit: they could guide the water but could not locate someone beyond the wall. In this example, the player wants that experience to influence future acquisitions. They might pursue an appropriate sense, train a useful practice, improve a known working, or learn to prepare better ordinary tools. Advancement does not require abandoning the character’s identity for a prescribed career. Ask which recurring problem the character now cares about and what actual rule or practical habit would make their next contribution more understandable.

sections.title: Budget and purchases are different records
sections.text: The progression reference gives a cumulative acquisition allowance. The purchase ledger records what the character has actually acquired. Do not add a cumulative table value to the previous allowance as if it were an increment, and do not count spent BU as a new second progression total. Ordinary unspent BU, valid mirror credit, and actual debt used remain distinct. Item BU stays separate. The DM and players agree rewards and pacing; there is no compulsory per-session schedule that must be invented to make a campaign function. State which progression reference and agreement the table uses.

sections.title: A conversation after the rescue
sections.text: Player: “I want to learn a sense that could locate someone behind a partition.” DM: “Describe the information and medium you want. What blocks it?” Player: “I imagine contact through a continuous surface, not reading thoughts or seeing all equipment.” Companion: “Then we can compare it with the existing contact-sense examples.” The proposed acquisition is still reviewed for its actual scope and price. The scene supplies a reason to learn, not automatic permission. A narrow intelligible grant can serve the concept more reliably than a powerful title whose limits nobody can explain.

sections.title: Reorganizing is not repurchasing
sections.text: The player gives an existing working a clearer capability name and moves its references into a heritage reflecting new responsibilities. If no actual acquisition changed, the underlying purchase count does not multiply. If the new record adds a sense, numerical bonus, or other genuine rule, record that addition and its agreed accounting. Keep a note of the adopted version where it matters. Rewriting a biography can alter what the character values without granting extra mechanics; replacing an ingredient can alter mechanics without requiring the entire biography to disappear. Review the two kinds of change separately.

sections.title: A drawback must remain a real choice
sections.text: A player may propose an eligible personal drawback with mirror credit. Read its actual consequence, recipient, condition, and ending terms. A descriptive dislike does not automatically produce budget. A debt ceiling limits what may be used; it is not free credit. Reusing the drawback inside several compositions does not erase it or create unlimited new credit. An ally’s benefit does not remove a restriction on the character who accepted it. These distinctions help the group assess whether the drawback will genuinely appear in play. If it will not, revise the proposal instead of treating accounting as a substitute for agreement.

sections.title: The sheet grows, but does not heal itself
sections.text: When advancement changes derived values, review the actual current attributes, applicable training, defenses, and maximum Vitality. Raising maximum Vitality does not automatically restore current Vitality. An explicit bonus has its own conditions; a proficiency grant does not become another copy of PB merely because the character already has training. If a new acquisition introduces advantage, use the net-stack rule rather than folding it into an unexplained numerical modifier. A short before-and-after review catches practical misunderstandings while preserving the useful history of how the character learned.

sections.title: The exercise: choose one next lesson
sections.text: Name a scene your character recently struggled with. Write the desired improvement, an existing or proposed ingredient that genuinely supports it, and one limit that remains afterward. For the bridge rescuer, a contact sense may improve location through its stated medium while leaving reach, delivery, and healing unchanged. Explain a future use and a use outside its scope. Then check the purchase ledger and table agreement. The answer should connect story, actual permission, and accounting. You do not need to solve every future problem at once; one well-understood acquisition can make the next adventure feel different.

imagePurpose: The makers’ workshop becomes a scene of reflection and altered plans. Show a familiar working being revised, supporting continuity of concept rather than depicting advancement as an unrelated arsenal.

quickFacts.label: Continuity
quickFacts.value: Let a remembered scene guide a specific acquisition.

quickFacts.label: Audit
quickFacts.value: Cumulative allowance, actual purchases, Item BU, credit, and current resources stay distinct.

title: Play with paper, not a second app

sections.title: Keep the information a human needs
sections.text: You can play without the platform open. In this example, the party takes paper records to a table with limited space. The useful character page holds current values, applicable check totals, owned permissions, important equipment, and active consequences. Supporting pages preserve actual ingredient definitions and version notes where needed. A list of impressive names alone is not enough to explain a working. Conversely, printing every public catalogue entry is unnecessary. Choose the content the character actually uses and make it available in a form its player can comfortably read.

sections.title: Three records prevent confusion
sections.text: Separate the enduring character record, the purchase ledger, and the scene state. The character record explains actual rules and current derived values. The ledger identifies acquisitions and separate Item BU accounting. Scene state tracks current Vitality, movement used, Reaction Slot availability, active workings, and consequences. These can fit on one sheet or several, depending on the reader. Their separation is conceptual, not a compulsory page count. Erasing a spent reaction should not accidentally delete an acquired rule; renaming a capability should not erase a consequence still affecting the character.

sections.title: A conversation before play
sections.text: Player: “My working card has the ingredient definitions on the back. Here is the normal use, and here is the targeting limit.” Companion: “Can I read that limit aloud when we plan?” Player: “Yes. My scene note tracks whether it is currently maintained.” The table has enough information to discuss a future use. This example does not require every player to perform a speech or expose private character notes. It shows how a short readable record can support cooperation. A player may prefer a quiet written description, a spoken summary, or another comfortable way of sharing the necessary facts.

sections.title: Show position without a compulsory map
sections.text: For a complicated crossing, sketch the bank, landing, line, and known recipients. Label what blocks sight or delivery and which support is secure. For a conversation, a short list of people and promises may be more useful than a battle map. Use the representation that explains the actual uncertainty. A rough drawing need not introduce precise grid mechanics the table has not adopted. If someone cannot see the diagram, describe the relevant relationships aloud. The shared scene is the important result; the drawing is a tool to help everyone understand it.

sections.title: Make changing state easy to change
sections.text: Use a pencil, tokens, separate cards, or another familiar method for temporary state. A token can show a spent Reaction Slot; a short note can show the next upkeep point and ending condition. Spell out the token’s meaning rather than expecting everyone to recognize a color. Keep current and maximum Vitality distinct, alongside the short-rest recovery still available. Write actual ending conditions for lasting consequences. A new Council clears the appropriate round markers, not every persistent restriction. This prevents a tidy table from becoming a mechanically misleading table.

sections.title: Adjust the presentation to the player
sections.text: Someone may need larger text, stronger contrast, more room between lines, or a spoken explanation. Someone else may prefer a compact card with details on a second sheet. These changes need not remove rules or change the character. Avoid using decorative script for long instructions or relying on an illustration to convey a necessary limit. Read an important agreement aloud if that helps, and let the player verify the record. Accessible play comes from making the actual information available without demanding the same reading speed, memory, or style of performance from every person.

sections.title: The exercise: hand over one working
sections.text: Give a companion the record of one frequently used capability without explaining it first. Ask them to identify the subject, behavior, targeting method, reach, continuing terms, and actual consequence. If they cannot find an answer, improve the record or include the missing ingredient definition. Do not ask them to guess from the artwork or title. Next, show the separate purchase entry and explain which references point to that same acquisition. The exercise succeeds when another human can apply the real working in a changed scene. A beautiful record is most useful when its beauty makes those answers easier to find.

imagePurpose: Use the transparent map, lantern, and writing objects as a small margin composition beside a paper-record example. The image reinforces practical offline play and must not become another required digital tool.

quickFacts.label: Offline essentials
quickFacts.value: Actual rules, acquisition identity, current state, and ending conditions.

quickFacts.label: Presentation
quickFacts.value: Use a readable format that fits the person and the table.
